body_markdown:
Not counting roller skates, I got my first wheels at the age of 13. The rollers in question were on a Humber bicycle, manufactured by the same company that made Humber automobiles, such as the famed Super Snipe: the Rootes Group. I was four or five in 1940 and 1941 in World War II, and even from that tender age I was obsessed with the Royal Air Force and its Staff Cars. I could recite the ranks of the Royal Air Force; I drew sketches of Spitfires and Hurricanes and Spitfires and Hurricanes and, of course, Humber Super Snipe Staff cars were on my radar.


## Super Snipes in the Military


Wiki Commons


Rootes Humber cars were up there in the luxury class. Throughout World War II, the company’s chauffeur-driven Humber Super Snipes transported Prime Minister Winston Churchill (it was his favorite car), cabinet ministers, high-ranking army and navy officers, R.A.F. Air Chief Marshals, Air Marshals, Air Vice Marshals, Air Commodores, Group Captains, Wing Commanders and even Squadron Leaders.


The WWII-era Humber Super Snipe of WWII was a large executive car, packing a 4086 cc straight-six side-valve engine that made 100 hp at 3400 rpm. At 79 mph, it was also one of the fastest cars of its era. The engine’s design had a lot of American influence. Delmar “Barney” Roos—who had left a successful career at Studebaker to join the Rootes Group in 1936—contributed significantly to the Super Snipe’s engineering. This gave it something of an American character: large, smooth, powerful, and relatively refined for its time.


Autocar/LAT Images


Rootes built 1500 Super Snipes for use as Staff Cars, modified with increased ground clearance; a wider front track; and larger, low-pressure Dunlop tires. Specialist car body builders Thrupp & Maberly built the Desert Open Tourer/Convertible version for high-ranking commanders and the Long-Range Victory Car, featuring larger fuel tanks, mine-proof floors, and enlarged front mudguards.


Motor/LAT Images/Getty Images


Several Humber military variants using the Super Snipe engine, chassis, running gear, and other components were built, although in relatively small numbers: 1500 to 5000 examples between 1940 and 1945. I can safely deduce that the Rootes Humber Super Snipe was unique in this regard; it’s a blip compared with the Willys Jeep (one car built in two versions: the Willys Overland, and the Ford GPW variant) of which more than 640,000 were built between 1941 and 1945.


## Humberette LRC


Royal Air Force


There was variety among the military Humbers. I’ll start with the Humber Light Reconnaissance Car (LRC), also known as the Humberette. This was a heavily armored car built on the Super Snipe chassis, engine, and running gear. It had the larger Dunlop low-pressure tires and four-wheel drive—selectable using a lever. It weighed over 6700 pounds. The turret was equipped with a main anti-tank gun and a Bren light machine gun.


At 75 miles per hour, it must have been the fastest armored car on record. Mind you, carrying all that weight, it would have taken some time to get up to such speed. The power-to-weight ratio was a lowly 29 hp per ton. It must have been a pig to drive, especially given the narrow slots to see through. The LRC had a crew of three: a Commander/Gunner, a Driver, and an Operator/Wireless Operator. It was equipped with a Smoke Discharger to confuse any enemy chasing it.


## The “Humber Box”: FWD/Heavy Utility 4×4


Flickr/macspite


The Humber FWD, or Heavy Utility 4×4, was used as a general-purpose and Staff car, employing the chassis, engine, and many components from the Super Snipe. It was also equipped with the larger low-pressure Dunlop tires. In general-purpose mode, it could be a command car, mobile radio/wireless car, a two-stretcher field ambulance (built by Thrupp & Maberly), or a minibus seating six to eight people. It was nicknamed the “Humber Box.”


## Humber Scout 4×4


Wiki Commons


Another military vehicle using Super Snipe engine and components was the Humber Scout car, a 4×4 with larger wheels and tires for fast cross-country use. It was lightly armored and weighed a thousand pounds less than the LRC. It carried a crew of two, with an emergency seat for a third member, and was equipped with radio and a Bren light machine gun. A second light machine gun could be mounted above the roof and operated remotely inside the vehicle using a what looked like bicycle handlebars that steered to aim—with the brake lever firing the machine gun!


Talk about necessity being the mother of invention. No peering through slots for the driver; it had a small proper windshield. The Scout Car did nort of 60 mph cross-country, so it could get out of trouble quickly.


## Desert Open Tourer


Wiki Commons


I discovered towards the war’s end that Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery (popularly known as “Monty”), used a Desert Open Tourer Humber Super Snipe as his mobile headquarters across North Africa, Sicily, and Italy. A second, almost identical car, called the Victory car, he used in North-West Europe after D-Day. Monty nicknamed the Victory car ‘Old Faithful’ after it fell in the sea off a Mulberry Harbor post-D-Day; it was running again 24 hours later. (The desert car is on display at the Imperial War Museum in London, and the Victory car is in the Coventry Motor Museum.)


## A Humble ’70 Humber for Yours Truly


Despite my wartime childhood admiration, I didn’t buy a Humber car until 1970. It was a low-mileage 1967 Series V Super Snipe Estate (Station Wagon). For a British car, it was big at 188 inches long and heavy at 3600 pounds. The engine was designed by the British aircraft and car engine manufacturer Armstrong Siddeley—an inline OHV six-cylinder displacing 2965 cc. It used twin Zenith Stromberg 175CD carburetors and a Harry Weslake-tuned cylinder head to output 137.5 bhp at 4800 rpm. Top speed of the car was said to be 100 mph, and zero to 60 mph took 12.5 seconds. Allegedly.


Wiki Commons/Redsimon


“Said to be,” I mention for top speed because I never dared to take it above 85 mph, for reasons I detail below, and “allegedly” for 0 to 60 mph because it never felt that quick. It had a three-speed column shift manual gearbox with Laycock de Normanville overdrive. The clutch was very heavy, but I didn’t need to use it that much. The high engine torque came in at around 1800 rpm, so once the car was up to 30 mph, I put it into overdrive third and left it there.


My Super Snipe boasted “Hydrosteer” power-assisted steering, which felt okay but a bit vague up to about 70 mph; any faster than that and the car really started to wander, making it difficult to place on the road. At that point it felt a lot more “hydro” than “steer.” At over 80 mph on the German Autobahn I was applying correction, and as the speed increased, so did the amount of correction, until my hands were constantly on the move. I rarely took it over 80 mph.


Ivan Berg


It was a comfortable car, I remember. The suspension was soft, even spongy, soaking up most road imperfections with ease. The front suspension had independent coil springs with wishbones and anti-roll bar; rear suspension was more old hat: leaf springs, telescopic dampers, and a live axle. Disc front brakes and drum rear, so good stopping, but with a lot of front dip under braking. Handling not suited to anything spirited. The body rolled, even at the mere hint of a corner, and it understeered, and the axle tramped if you floored the accelerator in second gear, while attempting to power-drive through a corner. (Something I only did once!) With slippery leather bench seats and no seatbelts, an attempted fast corner could deposit your companion on your lap. You could say I drove it sedately.


In keeping with its luxury appeal, the car had a heater. Air conditioning was an option reserved for the U.S. market, though very few Super Snipes made it across the Atlantic. Premium leather bench seating paired nicely with front and rear and walnut dashboard and door trim. Soft and thick wool carpets. Pull-down walnut picnic tables were nice for the rear passengers.


## A Quasi-American Tradition


Daily Express/Hulton Archive/Getty Images


Rootes was already talking to Chrysler about a merger at the time, and the Super Snipe’s body style reflected this. The quad headlights were borrowed from the Chrysler 1957/8 model year, in fact. With its curved windshield, quad headlights, and wrap-around full-width grille, the front of the Humber looked positively American.


Road testers at the time thought it looked a lot like a smaller 1955 Chevrolet Nomad wagon. There was even a[plan to offer a version of the Super Snipe with a U.S. Chrysler V-8.](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/humber-imperial-v8-a-chrysler-powered-british-luxury-sedan-that-didnt-pan-out/) Twelve V-8 cars were built (six engineering prototypes and six pre-production cars) and were used by the Rootes family and executives.


Lord Rootes’s brother Reginald Rootes was chauffeured around in one of the pre-production cars for many years. The car survived and at the time of writing is on display in the Isle of Man Motor Museum. The cars were never road-tested by the British *Autocar* or *Motor* magazines, but the 218 bhp 273-cubic-inch Chrysler V-8 using a four-barrel Carter carburetor would have been good for at least 118/120 mph, with much better acceleration.


Victor Blackman/Getty Images


The final Super Snipes were made in 1967. Rootes was in trouble financially and Chrysler bought the company. And that was the end of Humber.


## Super Sniping from Behind the Lens


I bought my Humber because I thought it would make a stable camera platform. I sent it to a specialist camera car conversion company. That outfit customized the Humber with a non-slip roof platform that included built-in tripod mounts and latches. The roof was accessible via a ladder mounted behind the passenger side rear door. It all added a good bit of weight and wind resistance, but I wasn’t planning to break any speed records. Autobahn cruising between 75 and 80 miles an hour was its sweet spot, and the Hydrosteer power steering almost behaved. It was quiet, and for its time, a refined vehicle.


Ivan Berg


It was a good platform for still photography but proved useless for filming on the move. That was aother car’s domain: the Citroën DS Safari with its hydropneumatic self-leveling suspension. The Humber, or indeed any vehicle, couldn’t compete.


Once, I drove my Super Snipe to Denmark once for one of our annual family holidays, took it to the beach, and got it stuck it in the sand. I had to wait for a fisherman’s tractor to tow me out. (Monty’s low-pressure desert balloon tires would have got me out[PDQ](https://www.dictionary.com/browse/pdq) ). But that’s another story.
